summary: At just 4.6 square miles with roughly 25,000 residents, Mountain House is one of California's most meticulously planned master communities — a town that didn't exist before the early 2000s, built almost entirely from scratch on flat San Joaquin Valley farmland west of Tracy. The geography is wide-open agricultural horizon in every direction, with distant views of the Altamont Pass wind turbines to the west and the Diablo Range beyond; sunsets here light up an enormous sky unbroken by hills or tall structures. That openness comes with a tradeoff: this is a textbook bedroom community, with very few local employers — most working residents commute west through the Altamont toward the Tri-Valley or Bay Area, a drive that can stretch well past an hour each way during peak traffic on I-580. The median household income of nearly $172,000 against an $860,000 median home value yields a price-to-income ratio around 5:1, notably more accessible than the Bay Area cities many commuters left behind, though rent at $3,232 per month still commands a serious share of income. The built environment is almost entirely post-2000 subdivisions connected by looping streets, planned parks, and man-made lakes — cohesive in design but light on walkable retail or independent restaurants, with most errands requiring a car trip to Tracy or beyond. With average daily highs around 74°F, over nine hours of sunshine, and that 2.7% poverty rate, the material comfort is real — but Mountain House's defining equation is trading proximity and urban texture for newer housing and open sky.
